newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica JSE faces rocky H1, brighter H2-Old Mutual.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica JSE faces rocky H1, brighter H2-Old Mutual.

text.p: South African shares could be in for a rocky ride on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) in the first half of 1997 but prospects are bright for a more buoyant second half, Old Mutual said on Thursday.

"While the first half of this year might be difficult for the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, prospects could improve considerably in the second six months," Adrian Allardice, senior portfolio manager at Old Mutual Unit Trusts told a news conference.
"In fact, 1997 may yet turn out to be a good year for the stockmarket," he added.

The slowdown of the South African economy and resultant effect on corporate earnings would see stock prices come under early pressure, but prospects for better growth in 1998 would boost prices later this year, Allardice said.
However, he warned that there were a host of factors that could upset the pattern and the market would still be prone to volatility.
"The market will remain volatile. We are open to the rest of the world now and we are small in size in their eyes. They tend to either love us or hate us," he said.
The performance of Wall Street has been eagerly watched as South African shares tend to follow New York, which has been on a recent bullish run.
"Stronger United States economic growth could lead to U.S. interest rates being hiked and an ensuing correction in the Dow which would rebound on local markets," Allardice said.
Other important factors which could boost or dampen the JSE are government actions such as the upcoming March budget and moves towards privatisation.

One of the key plans of government economic reform is a budget deficit target of four percent and Allardice said he expected a tough budget from finance minister Trevor Manuel that would aim to ensure this.
"The government is very intent on keeping the budget deficit under control," he said.

Two things that could provide an extra fillip to South African shares in 1997 are an agriculture sector set to get a healthy boost from heavy rains and progress the government might make on privatisation.

Investors have criticised South Africa for its slow march to privatising state-owned assets. Allardice said the government was moving in the right direction, but 1997 would have to be the year when words were turned into firm action.
"This year will be the test year as to how fast and to how thoroughly the government will move on privatisation," he said.

The South African government has now formally invited four potential overseas buyers to submit detailed bids for a 20 to 30 percent stake in telecommunications utility Telkom -- the first major privatisation.
